passage: The polytechnic in Hosur had given its prize for the best working model to Anand's team: a small solar pump that lifted water from a bucket into a clay pot. That evening the principal called each of the three boys in, one by one, to write a line for the college newsletter about who did what. Anand said he had designed the pump and done "most of it." Kamal said he had wired the solar panel and fixed the leaks, "which was really the hard part." The third boy said the pump would never have run without his gearbox. The principal smiled and opened the lab register, where each boy signed in and out and wrote what he worked on. Anand's signature was there on eleven days. Kamal's on fourteen. The third boy's on twelve. Nobody had done most of it.

qa.q: What did the team's solar pump do?
qa.a: It lifted water from a bucket into a clay pot.

qa.q: Why did Anand feel sure he had done most of it?
qa.a: He felt proud of his design and remembered his own days clearly, so his part felt biggest, while the others' work stayed in the background.

qa.q: How did the lab register help settle the question?
qa.a: It gave a written record of who worked on which days, showing all three had worked about equally instead of relying on memory.

qa.q: How might Kamal feel when the register is opened?
qa.a: Kamal might feel a little embarrassed, since his claim of doing the hard part sat beside two teammates who had worked nearly as many days.

grounding: Shows each member of a college team privately claiming most of the credit until a written register shows the work was shared.

passage: The peer-evaluation forms for the marketing project at the university in Leeds were due by midnight. Emeka filled his in the library café: "My share of the work: 45%. I set up every meeting and wrote the pitch." Across town, Wei typed: "My share: 50%. I built the survey and ran all the numbers." Their third teammate, a quiet student from Poland, wrote 40%. The tutor, reading them the next day, added the numbers on a sticky note and called all three in. "You've done 135% of one project," she said. Emeka laughed, then stopped. He really had believed his number. So had Wei. The tutor handed them a blank task sheet. "Next time, you each log your hours as you go. I'll mark from this." Wei looked at Emeka. "I didn't know you did all the meeting notes." "I didn't know about the survey weekends."

qa.q: What share of the work did Wei claim?
qa.a: 50%. Wei built the survey and ran all the numbers.

qa.q: What was Emeka feeling when he laughed and then stopped?
qa.a: He felt amused and then uncomfortable, realising he had truly believed his own number though the shares made no sense together.

qa.q: What does the tutor ask them to do next time, and why?
qa.a: Log their hours as they go on a task sheet, so recognition comes from a written record rather than each person's memory.

qa.q: How might the quiet teammate see the tutor's sticky note?
qa.a: The teammate might feel relieved, since the sum showed that everyone had overestimated, not only one person.

grounding: Shows each member of a university team believing they did the most, so their claimed shares add up far beyond the whole project.

passage:
Launch day, Tuesday. The new booking page Binita's team built went live at ten. By evening, sign-ups were double the target. People kept messaging her: "You're a genius!"
Thursday, team meeting. Binita didn't take the bow. "Three things," she said, on the whiteboard. "What I did well: I pushed us to test with real users early. What was luck: a travel blogger happened to share us on Tuesday; we didn't plan that. What I got wrong: I set the deadline too tight, and Raghav worked two late nights because of it." She turned to Raghav. "Thank you. The payment fix was yours."
The next Monday. In her written report to the director, she used the same three headings. The director replied: "Most honest launch report I've read." Raghav, cc'd, sent Binita a single thumbs-up.

qa.q: What did Binita write under 'what was luck'?
qa.a: A travel blogger happened to share us on Tuesday; we didn't plan that.

qa.q: How might Raghav have felt when Binita thanked him?
qa.a: Raghav probably felt seen and appreciated, especially after two late nights caused by the tight deadline.

qa.q: Which part of Binita's approach builds trust, and why?
qa.a: Naming her own good call, the luck and her mistake side by side, because the team can see she won't take credit that isn't hers.

qa.q: What would change if Binita had simply accepted "You're a genius"?
qa.a: The team's work and the lucky share would go unseen, and the tight-deadline mistake might happen again.

grounding: Shows a professional naming what she did well, what luck helped and what she got wrong, and thanking a colleague honestly after a success.

passage: Suraj, you've been praised all week for your first big story, and you're glowing. Good. Now let your Reena Maasi tell you something. When I was your age at the newspaper in Nagpur, my article on the water tankers made the front page. The editor called it the best piece of the year. I wanted so badly to say it was all me. But at the office party, when they raised a glass, I said three things. I found the story by listening to the women at the tap every morning for two weeks; that part was mine. A tanker driver happened to speak to me the day his boss was away; that was luck. And I spelled the councillor's name wrong in the second paragraph. Then I thanked our photographer, whose picture sold the story more than my words. People trusted me more after that, not less.

qa.q: Where did Reena Maasi's article make the front page?
qa.a: At the newspaper in Nagpur.

qa.q: What was young Reena feeling when the editor praised her article?
qa.a: She felt proud and tempted, wanting badly to say the success was all hers.

qa.q: Which choice in the story built trust, and why?
qa.a: At the office party she named her own effort, the luck and her mistake, and thanked the photographer, showing she would share credit honestly.

qa.q: How might the photographer have felt at the office party?
qa.a: The photographer likely felt valued and surprised to be publicly thanked for the picture that sold the story.

grounding: An elder recalls naming her own effort, the luck involved and a mistake, and thanking a colleague, after her first big success.

passage: Devika had two minutes on stage and the microphone kept cutting out. The regional award for the flood-relief project was in her hand, and the hall in Guwahati was noisy with clapping. The host whispered, "Quickly, please, we're behind time." She could have just said thank you. Instead she leaned into the crackling mic. "What we did well: we mapped every village before the rain, and I'm proud of that. What was luck: the second flood came two days later than forecast, which gave us time. What I got wrong: I sent the first boats to the wrong bank, and we lost a morning." The mic died. She raised her voice. "And Kavitha, who ran the supply kitchen for twenty days straight, deserves this more than I do." Kavitha, in the third row, covered her face with both hands.

qa.q: How many days did Kavitha run the supply kitchen?
qa.a: Twenty days straight.

qa.q: Why did Devika raise her voice after the mic died?
qa.a: She felt determined not to let the thanks be lost, wanting everyone to hear Kavitha's part even under time pressure.

qa.q: What makes Devika's short speech a fair way to take credit?
qa.a: She names her real achievement, the lucky delay and her own mistake, then thanks Kavitha, so no one gets more or less credit than they earned.

qa.q: What is it like for Kavitha to hear her name from the stage?
qa.a: Kavitha seems overwhelmed and moved, covering her face, after twenty hard days that might have gone unnoticed.

grounding: Shows a professional, under time pressure, naming her own success, the luck and her mistake, and honestly thanking a colleague.

passage: Gabriel was late for the school bus in Lisbon, and when the bell rang he shoved past Tiago at the classroom door. "Sorry, I'm in a hurry!" he called over his shoulder. At lunch the canteen line was long. Tiago stepped back to let someone pass and knocked Gabriel's tray. Juice everywhere. "You did that because you're rude," Gabriel said. "You always push." That evening, telling his sister Beatriz about it, he said, "Tiago is so rude. He pushes everyone." Beatriz raised her eyebrows. "And this morning at the door?" "That was different. I was late for the bus." "So when you push, it's the bus. When Tiago pushes, it's Tiago?" Gabriel opened his mouth, then closed it and went to find his football.

qa.q: What did Tiago knock at lunch?
qa.a: Gabriel's tray.

qa.q: Why was Gabriel so annoyed with Tiago?
qa.a: Covered in juice, Gabriel felt angry and decided Tiago was simply rude, not noticing the long, crowded canteen line.

qa.q: What question helped Gabriel see his double standard, and what could he try next time?
qa.a: Beatriz asked about the morning push; next time Gabriel could look for a hurry or a crowd behind someone else's push, as he does for his own.

qa.q: How might Tiago see what happened in the canteen?
qa.a: Tiago probably saw it as an accident while stepping back to let someone pass, and felt unfairly called rude.

grounding: Shows a child explaining his own push by being in a hurry but calling another boy's push a sign that he is rude.

passage: The swimming club's changing room was steamy and packed after the Saturday class. Omkar, shivering, pushed ahead of Dorje to get to the warm shower. "I'm freezing," he said. Five minutes later, Dorje, dripping, bumped past Omkar at the lockers. "Hey! Stop pushing, you're so rude," Omkar snapped. Pema ma'am, the coach, was folding towels by the door. "Omkar, why did you push at the shower?" "Because I was cold!" "Why do you think Dorje pushed at the lockers?" "Because he's rude. He's always like that." "Is he always like that?" Omkar thought. Dorje had shared his goggles last week. "No..." "It's crowded, everyone's cold," Pema ma'am said. "Maybe Dorje is cold too." Omkar looked over. Dorje's lips were blue.

qa.q: Why did Omkar push ahead to the shower?
qa.a: Because he was cold; he was shivering and said, "I'm freezing."

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling when Dorje bumped past him at the lockers?
qa.a: He felt irritated and quickly decided Dorje was rude, while he saw his own push as only about being cold.

qa.q: How did Pema ma'am help, and what could Omkar ask himself next time?
qa.a: She asked why each of them pushed; next time Omkar could ask whether the other child might be cold or rushed, just like him.

qa.q: What is it like for Dorje to be called rude in the changing room?
qa.a: Dorje was likely cold and hurrying too, so being called rude would feel unfair after sharing his goggles only last week.

grounding: Shows a child excusing his own push because he was cold while calling another child's push rude, in a crowded swimming-club changing room.

passage:
Monday. At the park gate, Hrithik pushed Bittu out of the way to reach the swing first. "I only had ten minutes before tuition!" he told Rashmi didi, his tutor.
Wednesday. Bittu pushed Hrithik at the slide. Hrithik stormed into tuition. "Bittu is such a rude boy. He has no manners." Rashmi didi only said, "Hmm. Write that down for me."
Saturday. Rashmi didi gave him a small worksheet. Two lines. "Monday: Hrithik pushed because ______." "Wednesday: Bittu pushed because ______." Hrithik filled the first quickly: "I was in a hurry." The second, he started to write "he is rude," and stopped. He thought about the slide queue. It had been long, and Bittu's mother was calling him home. He wrote, "maybe he was in a hurry too."

qa.q: How many minutes did Hrithik say he had before tuition on Monday?
qa.a: He said he only had ten minutes before tuition.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling when he stormed into tuition on Wednesday?
qa.a: He felt angry and sure Bittu was simply a rude boy with no manners, forgetting his own push on Monday.

qa.q: How did Rashmi didi's worksheet help Hrithik?
qa.a: It put both pushes side by side, so he had to give Bittu a reason the same way he gave himself one.

qa.q: How might Bittu see the push at the slide?
qa.a: Bittu may have felt rushed because his mother was calling him home, not that he was being rude.

grounding: Shows over a week a child explaining his own push by hurry while calling another boy's push rude, until a worksheet puts them side by side.

passage: Uma, can I tell you something? Last night I had the biggest fight with Papa. I'm Abhinav, the calm one, remember? Right. So I shouted. I admit it. But I shouted because I've had boards stress for three weeks, no sleep, two mock tests. Papa shouted because he wants to control everything, like which tuition, what time I'm home. That's how it felt. Then this morning I heard him talking to Ma in the kitchen. He said, "I only raised my voice because I'm worried about his marks and the office is killing me. But that boy just screams at me because he's angry at the world." Uma, he said the exact opposite of me. His shouting was stress, mine was attitude. I stood there holding my toothbrush. We're both saying the same thing about ourselves.

qa.q: What did Abhinav hear Papa say in the kitchen?
qa.a: He only raised his voice because he's worried about his marks and the office is killing him.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling standing there holding the toothbrush?
qa.a: Abhinav felt stunned and uneasy, seeing that Papa excused his own shouting with stress just as Abhinav did, and blamed Abhinav's character.

qa.q: What could Abhinav try when they talk next?
qa.a: Abhinav could say what was stressing him and ask about Papa's office pressure, so both see each other's situation, not only temper.

qa.q: How does Papa see Abhinav's shouting?
qa.a: Papa sees it as anger at the world and attitude, not the stress of board exams that Abhinav feels.

grounding: Shows a teenager explaining his own shouting by stress and his father's by control, then overhearing his father say the exact opposite.

passage:
Monday. Thomas slammed his door so hard the calendar fell off. Mum had said no to the Goa trip with friends. "She just likes controlling me," he texted Yash. "I only yelled because I'm stressed about exams."
Wednesday. Yash was at their flat for maths. From the kitchen he heard Thomas's mum on the phone to someone: "I yelled back because I'm exhausted from double shifts. But Thomas, he just gets angry at everything these days." Yash pretended not to hear.
Saturday. Walking to cricket, Yash finally said it. "Your mum thinks she yelled because she's tired, and you yelled because you're angry." Thomas stopped. "That's backwards. I yelled because I'm stressed." "Yeah. And she thinks she yelled because she's tired." Thomas kicked a stone a long way. "So we both think we had reasons."

qa.q: What did Mum say no to on Monday?
qa.a: The Goa trip with friends.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling when he texted Yash on Monday?
qa.a: He felt angry and controlled, sure Mum's refusal was about control while his own yelling was only exam stress.

qa.q: What could Thomas and his mum each try in their next argument?
qa.a: Each could ask what the other is dealing with, like exams or double shifts, before deciding the other is just angry or controlling.

qa.q: How does Yash see the argument after Wednesday?
qa.a: Yash sees that both Thomas and his mum explain their own yelling by stress or tiredness and the other's by character.

grounding: Shows a teenager blaming his mother's shouting on control and his own on stress, while she sees it the other way round.

passage: Siddharth, beta, you slammed the door on your mother just now, and you think she's the only one who shouts. Let your Jasleen Dadi tell you a story. When I was sixteen in Amritsar, my own mother and I fought every single evening. I shouted because I was tired from school and scared about exams. She shouted, I was certain, because she wanted to rule my life. One night, after a fight about my hair, I found her little diary open on the sewing machine. I shouldn't have read it. I did. "Today I snapped at Jasleen because the grocer shouted at me and I had a fever. But she, she just has a temper now." Same fight. Same excuse. Only the names swapped. I closed it and sat on the stairs for an hour. That night I went back and said sorry first.

qa.q: Where did Jasleen Dadi find her mother's diary?
qa.a: Open on the sewing machine.

qa.q: What was young Jasleen feeling after reading the diary?
qa.a: She felt shaken and ashamed, seeing that her mother excused her own snapping with a bad day, just as Jasleen did, and blamed Jasleen's temper.

qa.q: Which choice in the story changed things between them?
qa.a: Going back that same night to say sorry first, after seeing both of them had their own reasons.

qa.q: How did Jasleen's mother see the evening fights?
qa.a: She saw her own snapping as caused by fever and the grocer, but saw Jasleen's shouting as a new temper.

grounding: An elder recalls, as a teenager, blaming her mother's shouting on control and her own on stress, then reading her mother's diary saying the reverse.

passage: Himani was still angry at midnight. Hrithik, her flatmate in the Koramangala flat, had left the sink full of dishes for the third day, and when she complained he'd snapped, "Not now." She opened a note on her phone and tried something her counsellor had suggested. First she wrote it as if it had happened to a friend: "A girl comes home tired and finds the sink full. She asks nicely and gets snapped at." Reading it that way, she noticed she had not asked nicely. She had banged a pan. Then she wrote it from Hrithik's seat: "I got home at eleven after a client call went badly. My flatmate banged a pan and started on the dishes before I'd even taken off my shoes." She sat back. Both people had been tired. Both had a reason.

qa.q: How many days had the dishes been in the sink?
qa.a: For the third day.

qa.q: What did Himani feel when she wrote the story as if it happened to a friend?
qa.a: She felt a jolt of discomfort, noticing she had banged a pan rather than asked nicely.

qa.q: Why does writing the scene from both seats help?
qa.a: It lets Himani see the situation behind both reactions, her tiredness and Hrithik's bad client call, instead of only his rudeness.

qa.q: How might Hrithik have experienced the moment he snapped "Not now"?
qa.a: He had just got home at eleven after a client call went badly, so a banged pan felt like an attack.

grounding: Shows a student retelling a conflict as if it happened to a friend and then from the other person's seat, finding situational reasons on both sides.

passage:
"Elizabeth, Joel ruined our lab report. He just deleted my section. He's so arrogant."
"Okay, Farida. Try something. Tell it to me like it happened to your cousin, not you."
"Fine. My cousin's lab partner deleted her section at midnight... without asking."
"Did he say anything?"
"He texted 'fixed formatting.' She didn't read the message. She just saw her work gone."
"Now tell it from his chair."
"Ugh. Okay. I'm Joel. The file won't open, it's midnight, the deadline is 9 a.m. Farida's part has broken tables that crash everything. I paste it into a new file and it loses half. I text her."
"And?"
"And... she replies with three angry voice notes."
"So?"
"So maybe he was panicking. And maybe I was panicking too."

qa.q: What did Joel text Farida?
qa.a: He texted 'fixed formatting.'

qa.q: What seems to shift in Farida as she tells it from Joel's chair?
qa.a: Farida's anger seems to soften into doubt, as she sees Joel may have been panicking over a broken file rather than being arrogant.

qa.q: Why does Elizabeth's two-step method work?
qa.a: Telling it first as a cousin's story and then from Joel's chair makes Farida look for the situation behind both reactions, not just blame.

qa.q: How might Joel have felt receiving three angry voice notes?
qa.a: Joel probably felt hurt and misjudged, having tried to save the file before a 9 a.m. deadline.

grounding: Shows a student retelling a conflict as if it happened to someone else and then from the other person's seat, finding reasons on both sides.

passage: After the college fest, I was furious with Ira. I'm Mohit, and I ran the stage schedule; she ran sound. Twice she started the music late, and the dance team blamed me. I wanted to tell everyone she was careless. Instead, the next morning, I tried something a senior once showed me. I wrote the whole evening down as if it happened to a friend: "Two students run a stage. One gets blamed for delays the other caused." Then I wrote it again from Ira's seat: "The schedule changes three times in an hour. Nobody tells sound. The mic batteries die and I'm alone backstage." When I read the second one, I remembered sending her the new schedule late. Twice. Neither of us was careless. We were both drowning. I texted her: "Coffee? I think we both had a terrible night."

qa.q: How many times did Ira start the music late?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling after reading the version from Ira's seat?
qa.a: Mohit felt humbled and a bit guilty, remembering sending the new schedule late twice, and the anger at Ira faded.

qa.q: How did Mohit handle the conflict well, and what could others learn from it?
qa.a: Mohit wrote the evening as a friend's story and then from Ira's seat before blaming anyone; others can do the same to find situational reasons on both sides.

qa.q: What was the fest evening like for Ira?
qa.a: Ira was alone backstage with dying mic batteries and a schedule that changed three times without anyone telling sound.

grounding: A student describes retelling a conflict as a friend's story and from the other person's seat, finding situational reasons on both sides.

passage:
Tuesday.
Hansa came in forty minutes late today, hair wet, saying the flyover was jammed after a truck broke down. Fair enough; it was on the news. Then at 11, the new trainee walked in twenty minutes late and Hansa said to him, in front of all of us, "This is about attitude. If you cared, you'd leave earlier." He said the bus hadn't come. She didn't even let him finish.
I kept thinking about it all afternoon. Same flyover. Same morning.
At five I asked Hansa, gently, if the trainee's bus might have been stuck on the flyover too. She went quiet. Then she said, "You're right. I gave myself the traffic and gave him the attitude." She walked over to his desk before she left.
Sunaina

qa.q: How late did the new trainee come in?
qa.a: Twenty minutes late.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling while thinking about it all afternoon?
qa.a: Sunaina felt uneasy and bothered by the unfairness, since Hansa had excused herself with traffic but blamed the trainee's attitude.

qa.q: How did Sunaina raise the issue, and why did it work?
qa.a: Sunaina asked Hansa gently and privately at five whether the trainee's bus might also have been stuck, which let Hansa see her double standard without being shamed.

qa.q: How might the trainee have felt when Hansa blamed his attitude in front of everyone?
qa.a: He likely felt humiliated and unheard, since he wasn't even allowed to finish explaining about the bus.

grounding: A colleague's diary shows Sunaina noticing that a manager blamed traffic for her own lateness but attitude for a trainee's, and gently pointing it out.

passage: At the sub post office in Sakleshpur, the postmaster was forty minutes late on Monday. "The ferry across the river was stuck," she said, fanning herself with a money-order form. Everyone nodded. On Wednesday the young postman came in late, soaked, his bag of letters wrapped in plastic. The postmaster didn't look up. "Some people simply don't take government work seriously." Keerthana, at the stamp counter, felt her stomach twist. The postman lived on the far bank. The ferry. She waited until the lunch break and set a cup of tea beside the postmaster's register. "Madam, did the ferry stick again today? He comes on it too." The postmaster paused with the cup halfway. Then she called the postman over. "Was it the ferry?" He nodded. "Next time, phone the office. I'll know."

qa.q: What did the postmaster say made her late on Monday?
qa.a: The ferry across the river was stuck.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when the postmaster blamed the postman?
qa.a: Keerthana felt her stomach twist with discomfort, seeing that the ferry excused the postmaster but not the postman.

qa.q: How did Keerthana raise the double standard, and what changed?
qa.a: She asked privately over tea whether the ferry had stuck again, which led the postmaster to ask the postman directly and set up a phone call instead of blame.

qa.q: How might the postman have felt when the postmaster finally asked him?
qa.a: He probably felt relieved and fairly treated after being called careless for the same delay she had faced.

grounding: Shows a clerk noticing that a postmaster blames a late postman's attitude but excuses her own lateness by the ferry, which leads to fairer feedback.

subtype: It will not happen to me [Actor]
passage: Last summer I was sure nothing bad could happen to me. I'm Baljeet, and my mother calls me her fearless boy. Abhinav said the high branch of the mango tree was too thin. "It'll break for you, not for me," I told him. I also said I'd never get caught skipping homework or fail the maths test. Bad things happen to other boys, I thought. On Sunday I climbed the high branch. It cracked. I slid down the trunk and scraped my whole arm. Abhinav ran for my mother; she cleaned it and made me promise to stay on the low branches. The same week I got caught about the homework, and I got a D in maths. Now when I think "not me," I remember that crack.

qa.q: What did Abhinav say about the high branch of the mango tree?
qa.a: Abhinav said it was too thin.

qa.q: Why was Baljeet so sure the branch would not break?
qa.a: He felt fearless and certain, believing bad things only happen to other boys, not to him.

qa.q: What could Baljeet do the next time he thinks "not me"?
qa.a: He could ask what would happen if it did happen to him, and listen when a friend like Abhinav warns him.

qa.q: How might Abhinav have felt when the branch cracked?
qa.a: Abhinav was probably frightened for his friend and relieved to be able to run for help.

grounding: A child looks back on being sure he would not fall, get caught or fail a test, because bad outcomes seemed to happen to other people.

subtype: It will not happen to me [Actor]
passage:
Class 3B, Thursday, teacher's note.
Before today's spelling test, Joseph told his table he did not need to study. "I never fail. Only the others fail." He also had a comic hidden in his desk and told Madhuri, who warned him, "Ma'am won't catch me. She never catches me." I did catch him, during the test. And he got four out of fifteen, the lowest in the class. He looked truly shocked. At break I sat with him. I asked, "What did you think would happen?" "Nothing bad. It doesn't happen to me." I asked him to make two lists with me: things that went well because he worked, and things that went badly when he didn't. Next week I'll check his study card each day.

qa.q: What score did Joseph get in the spelling test?

passage:
Monday.
Rode my bicycle down the Hill Road with no hands today. Shreya Appi said the brakes are loose and I'll crash. I won't. Only clumsy boys crash. I'm the best rider in our lane.
Tuesday.
Did it again. The front wheel wobbled a bit. Still fine. Nothing will happen to me.
Wednesday.
Shreya Appi told Abbu. I was so angry. Abbu took me to the cycle shop the same evening. The man said the brake cable was almost snapped. He fixed it while I watched. Abbu said, "No hands on Hill Road, beta. Not ever." I said the crash only happens to others. He said, "Everyone who crashed thought so too."
I didn't write anything back. But I looked at that almost-snapped cable for a long time.
Tanvir

passage:
Week 1, Monday. Ojas cycled to tuition on the highway service road without his helmet. "Helmets are for slow people," he told Swati at the gate. "Accidents happen to bad riders." The helmet hung on the hook at home.
Week 2, Thursday. A boy from the next batch came to tuition with his arm in a sling. He had been clipped by an auto at the same turn Ojas took every day. He had been a good rider too, everyone said. Ojas didn't say anything, but he rode home slower.
Week 3, Tuesday. Swati noticed the blue helmet on Ojas's head. "Changed your mind?" He shrugged. "My mother saw the boy's photo in the parents' group. She made me promise." A pause. "And I kept thinking, he also thought it wouldn't be him."

qa.a: He had been clipped by an auto at the same turn Ojas took every day and came with his arm in a sling.

qa.a: He felt confident and invulnerable, sure that accidents only happen to bad or slow riders.

qa.a: Seeing that a good rider was hurt at his own turn, and his mother's promise; seeing real cases close to home and a parent setting a clear rule can help others.

qa.a: Swati seems relieved and a bit surprised, noticing he now takes the risk seriously.

passage: Lalit, you think those boys racing bikes on the canal road are heroes? Sit, let your Rashmi Bua tell you about Meerut, when I was fifteen. My friends and I used to jump into the canal from the old bridge in July, when the water was high. Everyone said a boy had drowned there once. We laughed. That was a weak swimmer, we said. Not us. I jumped maybe twenty times that summer. Then one afternoon the current pulled me under the bridge. My friend's elder brother, who was fishing, pulled me out by my plait. I coughed water for an hour. At home my mother didn't shout. She just held me and went, that same evening, to tell the other girls' mothers. After that the bridge had a guard every monsoon. We weren't braver than that boy. We were just luckier, until I wasn't.

qa.q: Where did Rashmi Bua and her friends jump into the canal?
qa.a: From the old bridge.

qa.q: Why did young Rashmi laugh at the story of the boy who drowned?
qa.a: She felt fearless and sure it only happened to weak swimmers, not to her and her friends.

qa.q: Which moment in the story changed what happened at the bridge?
qa.a: Her mother going that same evening to tell the other girls' mothers, which led to a guard at the bridge every monsoon.

qa.q: How was the friend's elder brother affected that afternoon?
qa.a: He had to act fast to pull a drowning girl out, a frightening moment that showed the danger was real.

grounding: An elder recalls feeling as a teenager that the dangers of jumping into a canal were only for others, until she was nearly swept away.

passage: It was the night before the physics practical, rain drumming on the tin roof of the bus shelter where Jatin and Urmila were waiting. A boy from their class pulled out a small vape and passed it around. "It's just flavoured air," he said. Jatin reached for it. Urmila frowned. "You know the counsellor said it's still harmful." Jatin laughed. "That's for people who do it every day. I'm not going to get hooked. That happens to other people." The bus was twenty minutes late and the rain wasn't stopping. Urmila said quietly, "My cousin said that exactly. Now he can't get through the morning without it." Jatin paused, the vape halfway to his mouth. Then he handed it back. The next day Urmila walked with him to the counsellor's room, and he asked the questions he'd been too proud to ask.

qa.q: What did the boy say the vape was?
qa.a: It's just flavoured air.

qa.q: Why did Jatin think he would not get hooked?
qa.a: He felt confident and invulnerable, sure that harm happens to people who use it every day, not to him.

qa.q: What small step helped Jatin, and what could other teens try?
qa.a: Urmila's honest story about her cousin and going with him to the counsellor next day; others can ask a counsellor or trusted adult instead of trusting "not me".

qa.q: How might Urmila feel when Jatin hands the vape back?
qa.a: Urmila probably feels relieved and glad her quiet story about her cousin got through to him.

grounding: Shows a teenager believing the harm from vaping happens only to others, until a friend's real story and a counsellor help him think again.

passage: In Changanassery, everyone knew Siddharth would crack the state bank exam. He had topped his college. So when the notice came out, he applied for nothing else. "One attempt, that's all I need," he told his friend Thomas at the tea shop by the bus stand. He even told his father he'd start paying the house loan instalment from next year. Thomas, who had tried twice himself, stirred his tea. "Most people don't clear it the first time, Siddharth. Even toppers." "Most people aren't me." The results came in March. Siddharth had missed the cut-off by four marks. For a week he didn't leave his room. Then Thomas came over with two forms: the next attempt, and a job at the cooperative society in town. "Hope is fine," Thomas said. "But fill both."

qa.q: By how many marks did Siddharth miss the cut-off?
qa.a: By four marks.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when he said "Most people aren't me"?
qa.a: He felt proud and confident, sure that the usual odds didn't apply to him because he had topped his college.

passage: Thabo finished his engineering degree in Johannesburg in November and signed the lease on a flat in Rosebank the same week. It was expensive, but he'd have a job by January, obviously. Emil, his roommate from res, looked at the lease on the kitchen table. "No job yet, though?" "Three interviews. One will come through." "And if none do?" Thabo laughed. "Emil, I was top ten in my class. Plus Lerato says she'll move in by March, so rent gets halved." February came. Two rejections, one silence. Lerato took a post in Durban. Thabo sat on the floor of the half-empty flat with the rent reminder open on his phone. Emil came over with a pot of pap and said, "Tomorrow, the campus careers office. Together." Thabo nodded. For the first time, he made a list titled "Plan B."

passage: Ayesha stirred the vanilla into the batter at six in the morning in her Lucknow kitchen, before her half-day at the office. Her home cake business had eleven orders this month. She truly believed it would grow; she worked like it would. But on the fridge, under a magnet shaped like a cupcake, was a sheet titled "Just in case." It listed three things: keep the part-time office job until orders were steady for six months, a small cushion she'd set aside that she would not touch for ingredients, and a friend's café that had said they'd take her cakes if home orders dried up. Her brother Anirban, visiting, read it. "You don't believe in yourself?" "I do," Ayesha said, sliding the tin into the oven. "That's why I'm working this hard. The list is so a bad month hurts my plans, not me."

qa.q: How many orders did Ayesha's home cake business have this month?
qa.a: Eleven orders this month.

qa.q: What does Ayesha's answer to Anirban suggest she feels about her business?
qa.a: She feels hopeful and confident about the business, and calm, because the backup list protects her from a bad month.

qa.q: Which part of Ayesha's plan is wisest, and why?
qa.a: Keeping the part-time job and the café option alongside her hope, so a setback affects her plans rather than her sense of herself.

qa.q: Why might Anirban see the list differently from Ayesha?
qa.a: Anirban reads a backup plan as doubt, while for Ayesha it is simply part of working hard on a hopeful plan.

passage: Two years ago I applied for the fellowship in Berlin, and I'm writing this down because Vasudha asked me how I stayed calm. I'm Usha, a woman who is not calm by nature. I truly hoped I'd get it. I rewrote my proposal nine times; hope made me work harder. But I didn't bet everything on it. I kept my lab job and didn't tell them I might leave. I put aside a small cushion for visa fees and the flight, so if the answer was no, that money was still mine. And I made a Plan B: an application to a programme in Pune, less shiny but real. The answer from Berlin was no. I cried for one evening. Then I opened the Pune email. It was a yes. My plan was hurt, not me.

qa.q: How many times did Usha rewrite her proposal?
qa.a: Nine times.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when Berlin said no?
qa.a: Usha was sad enough to cry for one evening, but steady, because the Plan B and the cushion meant the no didn't break her.
